items.title: Etiological agent
items.contentHtml:
Onchocerca volvulus

  • Onchocerca volvulus is a filarial nematode transmitted by black fly bites.
  • The adult lodges in subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas) and releases microfilariae that migrate to the skin and eye.
  • The adult female can live 10-15 years; microfilariae 1-2 years.
  • Chronic disease is due to an inflammatory response against dead microfilariae, not the live parasite.
  • It is the second infectious cause of preventable blindness in the world.

items.title: Vector: Simulium
items.contentHtml:
Vector: Simulium (black fly)

  • The vector is the genus Simulium, known as black fly, which reproduces in fast-flowing rivers.
  • Transmission occurs when the female fly bites to feed on blood, inoculating infective larvae (L3).
  • The cycle is completed only in endemic areas with oxygenated water and vegetation; That is why the disease is associated with river blindness.
  • Vector control with larvicides reduces transmission, but is not the basis of individual treatment.

items.title: Microfilaria: distribution
items.contentHtml:
Microfilaria in skin and eye

  • The microfilariae of Onchocerca volvulus are found in the superficial dermis and in the anterior segment of the eye.
  • On the skin, they cause dermatitis and pruritus; in the eye, they cause keratitis, uveitis and chorioretinitis.
  • The load of microfilariae in the skin is quantified by serial biopsy: skin biopsy with reading of microfilariae per milligram of tissue.
  • Ocular migration is favored by chemotaxis towards the aqueous humor; The death of intraocular microfilariae triggers inflammation.

items.title: Onchocercoma
items.contentHtml:
Onchocercoma

  • The onchocercoma is a fibrous subcutaneous nodule that contains intertwined adult worms.
  • It is painless, mobile, 0.5-2 cm, located in bony prominences (iliac crest, ribs, skull).
  • In Africa it is located on the trunk and extremities; in America, especially in the head and upper part of the body.
  • Surgical removal of onchocercomas reduces the burden of microfilariae and is complementary to medical treatment.
  • The biopsy of the nodule shows adult worms and microfilariae, useful for definitive diagnosis.

items.title: Blindness due to sclerosing keratitis
items.contentHtml:
Sclerosing keratitis

  • Sclerosing keratitis is a chronic corneal opacification that leads to irreversible blindness.
  • Other ocular lesions: punctate keratitis, anterior uveitis, chorioretinitis and optic atrophy.
  • Blindness due to onchocerciasis is the most serious form; It is associated with a high parasite load and immune response.
  • River blindness is eponymous for the disease due to its high prevalence near rivers where the vector breeds.
  • Eye damage is secondary to the death of microfilariae in the eye, releasing antigens that induce inflammation.

items.title: Pruritus and dermatitis
items.contentHtml:
Intense pruritus and dermatitis

  • Intense pruritus is the most common symptom and can be disabling, often worse at night.
  • Chronic dermatitis evolves from pruritic papules to lichenification, hyperpigmentation and atrophy.
  • In endemic areas, leopard skin is described. (hypopigmentation) and elephant skin (thickening with folds).
  • Acute dermatitis due to massive death of microfilariae is observed after treatment (Mazzotti reaction).
  • The differential diagnosis includes scabies, atopic dermatitis and other filariases; but the endemic distribution guides.

items.title: skin biopsy
items.contentHtml:
Diagnosis: skin biopsy

  • The skin biopsy (snip) is the reference method: a superficial sample is taken with a scalpel or punch, placed in physiological saline and the emergence of microfilariae is observed.
  • 4 to 6 bilateral samples (iliac crest, scapula, calf) are taken to increase sensitivity.
  • The load It is expressed as microfilariae per milligram of skin; >10 microfilariae/mg indicates high density.
  • Sensitivity decreases in mild infections or after treatment; PCR on skin has greater sensitivity.
  • The Mazzotti test with diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is an alternative when the biopsy is negative, but causes a reaction.

items.title: Mazzotti test
items.contentHtml:
Mazzotti test

  • The Mazzotti test consists of administering an oral dose of diethylcarbamazine (DEC) and observing the appearance of pruritus, skin rash and eosinophilia in 24-48 hours.
  • The reaction occurs due to massive death of microfilariae, releasing antigens that induce inflammation.
  • It is useful when the skin biopsy is negative but there is clinical suspicion; however, it can cause serious reactions in patients with high ocular burden.
  • DEC is contraindicated in active ocular onchocerciasis due to the risk of exacerbation; That is why biopsy is preferred.
  • The Mazzotti reaction can also occur with ivermectin, but less intense.

items.title: Ivermectin
items.contentHtml:
Ivermectin: treatment of choice

  • ivermectin is the drug of choice for onchocerciasis; It is administered in a single oral dose of 150 µg/kg every 6-12 months.
  • It is effective against microfilariae, but does not eliminate adult worms; That is why it is repeated for 10-15 years (adult life).
  • Ivermectin should not be used in patients with high burden Loa loa coinfection, due to the risk of encephalopathy.
  • Massive administration in endemic communities reduces transmission and prevents blindness.
  • The dose is repeated until the skin biopsy is negative for at least 3 consecutive years.

items.title: Doxycycline and Wolbachia
items.contentHtml:
Doxycycline against Wolbachia

  • Wolbachia is an obligatory endosymbiont of Onchocerca volvulus; Without it, the worm cannot reproduce or survive.
  • Doxycycline at a dose of 100 mg/day for 6 weeks eliminates Wolbachia, sterilizes the females and reduces the production of microfilariae.
  • It is an indirect macrofilaricidal treatment, but it is not used as a first line in massive programs due to its duration and contraindications (pregnancy, children <9 years).
  • It is considered in patients who cannot receive ivermectin or in selected cases to reduce adult burden.
  • The combination of doxycycline with ivermectin may improve efficacy, but requires supervision.

items.title: Prevention
items.contentHtml:
Prevention: avoid Simulium bites

  • Primary prevention is based on avoiding Simulium bites using repellents, protective clothing and mosquito nets.
  • The vector bites during the day and outdoors, near rivers; That is why it is recommended to avoid activities during times of greatest vector activity.
  • Vector control with larvicides in rivers is an effective community measure.
  • Annual chemoprophylaxis with ivermectin in endemic communities reduces the prevalence of the disease.
  • Health education about the transmission cycle is key for prevention in endemic areas.

items.foco: Endemic in Africa and Latin America
items.title: Geographic distribution
items.contentHtml:
Endemic in Africa and Latin America

  • Onchocerciasis is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa (more than 99% of cases) and in foci of Latin America (Brazil, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico).
  • In Africa, the areas of greatest transmission are the valleys of fast-flowing rivers; hence the eponym river blindness.
  • In Latin America, the disease occurs in isolated foci in indigenous communities; Elimination has been achieved in several countries (Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico).
  • Migration and trade can introduce cases into non-endemic areas, but there is no transmission without the vector.
  • The diagnosis should be considered in travelers from endemic areas with pruritus, nodules or ocular symptoms.
